affSPR-desc:
Supremacy

The spirit has always been willing. The flesh has always been weak.—Comment, line 89, Category 2 bipedal locomotion protocol

A materialist ideology, believing that science is supreme and that technological progress must be prioritised above all else. They regard anything beyond scientific explanation as inherently useless, and their citizens readily replace flesh with machinery.

They blame childish religious wars and other failings of logic for the Great Mistake.
affHRM-desc:
Harmony

This world is a gift-garment that we wear upon ourselves and within ourselves, in gratitude to the giver.—From the Annunciation Rite of Polymorphalists

An ecologist ideology, believing that humanity must live in balance with nature, accepting limits on comfort and growth in the name of sustainability. Their citizens adapt themselves to the world rather than the world to themselves.

They blame over-industrialisation and the unsustainable nature of society for the Great Mistake.
affPRT-desc:
Purity

How much joy can this new world hold, when all I can think of is everything I've left behind?—Phaedra, Lamentation for Planetfall

A conservative ideology, believing that humanity must remain true to itself in both genetics and culture. Having lost so much, they cling to what remains of humanity's heritage, and see its preservation as the only way to stay human. Their citizens shun genetic modification and keep to traditional ways of life.

They blame the failure of long-held cultural values for the Great Mistake.
affNTR-desc:
Neutral

Beware, you who seek first and final principles, for you are trampling in the garden of an angry God and he awaits you just beyond the last theorem.—Sister Mariam Godwinson, But For the Grace of God

Not all societies have fully committed to a single affinity. Undecided ideologies, spanning obscure schools of thought, take the best of all worlds. Their citizens may modify their bodies as they wish, though not to the same extent as the others, and their combat is built on ancient doctrines of movement rather than raw technological advantage.

Many undecided countries place their own interests ahead of grand ideological struggles, and view space colonisation as humanity's best bet for surviving the centuries to come.
affMST-desc:
Mastery

We trusted the old world to hold. Never again will we trust what we did not build.—Aphorisms for Practical People

An environmental-engineering ideology, believing that humanity should have mastery over its surroundings. They seek to reshape ecosystems and make nature itself more resilient to our way of life.

They blame the fragility of the environment, and humanity's failure to adapt it to its will, for the Great Mistake.
affSYN-desc:
Synergy

Accepting the limitations of birthform betrays a lack of imagination.—Graffito within an abandoned city

An accelerationist ideology, believing that humanity must evolve and adapt to our new world, whatever the cost. Their citizens embrace radical change to both body and culture.

They blame unnecessarily conservative views of genetics and culture for preventing humanity from doing what needed to be done to avert the Great Mistake.
affDVN-desc:
Divinity

Go as I direct. Do as I bid. Why should my hand not control you? I see horizons you do not see. I make plans you cannot fathom.—Bhagavad 4

A spiritualist ideology, believing in the transcendence of the human mind and the importance of morality and ethics. They consider the spiritual and physical bodies separate entities, and so hold no strong feelings about genetics. Their societies are organised around faith and moral authority.

They blame rampant materialism and the rejection of faith and moral values for the Great Mistake.
MMA-desc:
MondayMarket is an independent index tracking the prices of raw materials traded worldwide. It consolidates reported market data into a single benchmark, giving governments, producers, and merchants a common measure of resource value—and a clear view of who holds leverage.

From metals and fuels to foodstuffs and industrial minerals, MondayMarket tracks availability, demand, and disruption across global supply chains. It does not set prices or broker trades. It tells the market what resources are worth, where they are scarce, and which regions can no longer afford to ignore the numbers.

Local prices may vary with transport, access, and regional conditions. The index records the difference; the market decides who pays for it.
MIT-desc:
The Münchner Institut für Technologie—also known as Müninstek—was founded in the late 21st century with a mission to research and develop solutions to the world's most pressing environmental challenges. Its founders recognized the urgent need to address issues such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource depletion, and they believed that scientific research and technological innovation could help pave the way for a more sustainable future.

The Müninstek quickly became one of the world's leading institutions for research on global ecology and sustainability. Its scientists and engineers worked on a wide range of projects, from developing new renewable energy technologies to designing more efficient and sustainable transportation systems. The Müninstek also had a strong focus on environmental policy and worked closely with governments and international organizations such as the INTEGR to promote policies that would help mitigate the effects of climate change.

The INTEGR is a European-based political and social organization with its headquarters located in Germany. It pursues austerity and radical change to prevent global warming from making Earth uninhabitable. The organization recognizes the importance of scientific research and technological innovation in achieving its goals together with the Institute, and it worked closely with the Müninstek on a range of initiatives aimed at promoting sustainable development and mitigating the effects of climate change.

One of the Müninstek's most significant contributions was its development of the Ecomodel, a comprehensive tool developed by the Institute for measuring and analyzing the environmental impact of various human activities. The model takes into account a wide range of factors, including energy consumption, resource usage, emissions, waste generation, and other environmental impacts.

The model is continuously updated with new data and insights, allowing for more accurate assessments of environmental impact over time. It has become a crucial tool for policymakers, businesses, and researchers around the world who are working to promote sustainable development and mitigate the effects of climate change.

The Ecomodel enables comprehensive monitoring of the current state and potential evolution of the ecology in any given region. In order to effectively use this model, the Müninstek has developed a range of classifications that are based on the overall quality of the ecology in a particular territory and other complex criteria known as Local Ecobalance Decay Level—or LED.

Each of these classifications represents a different level of ecological health, and some are more rare than others. For example, achieving no or very low ecobalance decay is extremely difficult, and it is rare for any state to attain this level. However, some governments have been able to refine their ecological advocacy measures and instruments to a point where they can maintain a level of ecological balance that is close to optimal. In contrast, other governments may need to intervene more directly in order to protect their territories from negative ecological changes. This can involve using conventional ecological engineering techniques to terraform the land and create artificial barriers against environmental degradation.

Overall, the Ecomodel and the Müninstek classifications provide a valuable framework for understanding and managing the complex ecology of different regions. By using this model and its associated tools, governments and other stakeholders can work together to ensure that the environment is protected and preserved for future generations.
LYS-desc:
Lyscore—Lys, Science, Culture et Ouverture—is Franco-Iberia’s independent cultural and historical corporation, built to make humanity’s memory impossible to erase. Publicly chartered and funded through a combination of state investment and private partnerships, it operates at arm’s length from the government: accountable to the public, but free to decide what it preserves, how it investigates, and where its work takes it.

Its mandate is vast: to seek out, recover and safeguard the records of human civilization wherever they remain—in public collections, private hands, threatened archives, abandoned settlements or the digital debris of a vanished world. Documents, artworks, scientific findings, oral histories and everyday objects all belong in its care. Each acquisition is authenticated, catalogued and preserved, then added to a secure, continually expanding archive accessible across borders.

Lyscore was founded on a conviction born from catastrophe: history cannot warn us if its evidence is lost, hidden or forgotten. Preservation, in its view, is not enough. Knowledge must circulate. Through open archives, traveling exhibitions, public campaigns, research fellowships and international cultural summits, Lyscore brings the past into active conversation with the present—and puts its findings within reach of citizens, scholars and decision-makers alike.

To its supporters, Lyscore is a shared vault for the memory of humankind. To its critics, it is an institution with an extraordinary power to shape what the world remembers. It accepts the burden that comes with that power: to preserve without claiming ownership, to inform without dictating conclusions, and to keep humanity’s record alive—even when the truth it contains is uncomfortable.
